name: PDO thread lift

card.summary: Absorbable polydioxanone threads inserted under the skin to lift sagging tissue; immediate improvement is reported, but long-term data are thin.
card.aka: thread lift, suture suspension, APTOS-style threads
card.note: Reviews describe mostly minor, short-lived adverse events but call long-term efficacy data lacking; practitioner training is unregulated in some countries.

quick.overview:
A PDO thread lift uses dissolvable polydioxanone sutures, sometimes with barbs or cones, placed beneath the skin to reposition or support sagging tissue in the midface, jowls or neck. It is performed in clinics without a surgical facelift incision.

In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a short-term way to get a sharper jawline or lifted cheeks. A 2025 systematic review found improvement on aesthetic scales immediately after treatment, while noting that previous studies had failed to show long-term efficacy for absorbable threads.
quick.mechanism: Threads are placed under the skin and anchored to tissue, mechanically suspending it. Absorbable materials such as PDO and poly-L-lactic acid dissolve over time, and a clinical study of PLLA/PLGA-containing threads found they stimulate collagen production in biopsies. Researchers differ on how much of any lasting effect comes from collagen stimulation versus mechanical lift.
quick.risks: Reviews describe mostly minor, self-limiting adverse events, such as bruising, swelling and asymmetry. A BBC investigation reported in Wikipedia found UK training courses with no mandatory qualifications and described poor infection control in an undercover recording; one physician quoted there called thread lifting the most dangerous aesthetic procedure because threads cannot be removed. PDO threads are medical devices administered by clinicians.

lead: A thread lift is a minimally invasive procedure that uses sutures, often barbed or cogged, inserted under the skin to suspend ptotic (sagging) tissue. PDO (polydioxanone) threads are absorbable and are the most commonly evaluated thread in recent reviews. [1][2]

A 2025 systematic review of twelve studies covering 818 patients reported that aesthetic scores such as the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale and FACE-Q improved in all cases immediately after the procedure, while stating that previous studies had failed to show long-term efficacy for absorbable threads. [1] A 2017 review concluded that results with barbed sutures were inconclusive and that adverse events were mostly minor and short-lived. [2]

Thread lifts are marketed as a lower-downtime alternative to surgical facelifts. Forum discussion in looksmaxxing communities frames them as a temporary lift or jawline enhancer, though no forum threads are cited here.

paras: Thread lifts suspend facial tissue using sutures. Earlier barbed non-absorbable threads have been largely supplemented by absorbable PDO and PLLA/PCL threads. [1][2][2] Wikipedia describes barbed silicone and APTOS ('anti-ptosis') threads as thread-lift variants. [3]

A Korean technique paper describes a vertical vector lift for Asian patients using wedge-shaped PDO sutures, popular in Korean aesthetic clinics. [4] Other techniques include mini-midface lifts with PDO cog threads. [5]

The 2025 systematic review reported immediate improvement on several scales across twelve studies, while noting long-term data remain limited. [1] A 2018 systematic review set out to establish the current state of the art on thread-lift sutures. [6] A 2009 long-term study of 33 patients evaluated outcomes of thread lifts alone or combined with other procedures. [7]

A review of Silhouette Instalift describes most patients as finding the lift immediately effective and pleased with enhancements. [8] A 2023 brow-region thread lift paper by Sahan and colleagues was later retracted by agreement between authors and journal. [9]

Human studies include a prospective single-center study of 25 volunteers, which examined biopsies and nasolabial fold severity after PLLA/PLGA-containing absorbable suspension sutures; the study reported collagen stimulation as its subject. [10] An observational study of thread lifts with Happy Lift reported outcomes in 37 procedures over 24 months. [11]

Registered trials include a comparison of PDO threads with a dermal filler for nasolabial folds and a performance and safety study of polydioxanone sutures for wrinkles and face lifting. [12][13] No registered randomized trials of long-term (multi-year) outcomes were identified.
A 2017 review found adverse events were mostly minor and self-limiting. [2] An update on absorbable thread lifts also reviewed complication reporting in twelve studies. [1]

Wikipedia reports a BBC investigation of UK thread-lift training, noting no mandatory qualifications and describing recordings of poor infection control and punctured blood vessels. [3] An anatomical study of transverse facial artery perforators has been used in discussions of vascular safety in midfacial procedures. [14]

timeline.event: Villa and colleagues publish an early review of thread-lift sutures, later updated in 2018. [6]
Systematic review re-evaluates the thread-lift literature. [6]
A brow thread-lift paper is published; it is retracted in 2024. [9]
Systematic review of absorbable facial thread lifts (2018-2022 literature). [1]
